cultivar: Local population plants and other cultivars suited to the appellation
processing: One bud with one or two leaves is fixed, rolled, dried and finished in a method close to pan-fired green, mixing traditional and modern steps.
harvest_season: Very early: picking and first sales can begin in early February, and lots are generally picked before Qingming.
appearance_dry: Tight, smooth, heavy strips with a dark, brownish green colour in the pan-fired style.
taste_profile: High, lasting chestnut aroma, a full mellow body and a long sweet aftertaste.

brewing.notes: General guidance for a pan-fired green. A little more heat brings out the chestnut, but keep steeps short for a strong style like this.

vintage_note: Its whole pitch is earliness: the new harvest reaches the market from about early February, well before most Chinese spring greens. Buy the current year and look at the picking date, because the appeal fades with time. The range covers about 13 products, from bud-grade to pre-Qingming leaf.
description:
Shuicheng Chun, literally Shuicheng spring tea, is a protected green from Shuicheng District in Liupanshui, western Guizhou. Its claim to fame is simple: it is early.

The gardens lie at about 1,200 to 2,200 metres, yet the harvest is said to open 10 to 15 days ahead of Guizhou's Zunyi and Tongren, and 10 to 25 days ahead of the Jiangsu and Zhejiang areas. Leaf is one bud with one or two leaves, and the finished style comes close to pan-fired green, tight and heavy.

In the cup, look for chestnut aroma, a mellow body and a long sweet finish in a bright yellow-green liquor. It has more weight than a delicate bud tea, but brew it as a green, with short steeps and water below boiling.

The name covers a range of about 13 products, including Yitianjian, Mingqian Cuiya and Fengyu, and these can be quite different, so compare the grade as well as the name. Selenium is promoted hard here too; judge the tea by the cup, not the claim.
history:
Little is documented about its earlier history. The national quality inspection authority approved geographical indication protection on 7 April 2015, covering 21 towns and townships of what was then Shuicheng County.

A provincial tea research institute test of the leaf is cited for its composition, and a draft provincial standard is listed in support of the indication.
